documents.unit: Center for Innovation in Teaching & Learning (CITL)
documents.title: Integrate AI into your Teaching
documents.summary: CITL's campus teaching-center page encourages instructors to integrate AI, lists benefits for faculty and students, and sets out ethical considerations. It sets no campus-wide rule and advises instructors to write course-specific boundaries instead of a blanket policy.
documents.stance_why: The page states no rule on student AI use. It says 'Define clear boundaries for AI use in course assignments and assessments' and advises against 'a blanket AI policy', leaving each instructor to decide, so the stance is delegates.

units.why: States the career reason for AI literacy: 'employers are expecting graduates to understand and use AI tools responsibly'. Coded P44 (AI as professional skill) and not P87 because the claim is about employers.
units.anchor: AI literacy is essential for future success because employers are expecting graduates

units.why: Says faculty 'are being asked to prepare students for a workforce where AI literacy will be essential, not optional', an expectation on instructors tied to careers, so P44.
units.anchor: are being asked to prepare students for a workforce where AI literacy will be essential

units.why: Invites faculty to 'model curiosity and adaptability by engaging with Generative AI'; a recommendation that instructors try AI themselves, which fits P63 (learning AI) better than P59 since it is about exploration, not a teaching task.
units.anchor: Faculty can model curiosity and adaptability by engaging with Generative AI

units.why: Frames the principle 'harness the benefits of AI while keeping higher education deeply human'; an institution-level statement of principle, so P56.
units.anchor: Our challenge is to harness the benefits of AI while keeping higher education deeply human

units.why: Says instructors 'can use AI to create the first draft of a course syllabus'; permission for faculty teaching work, so P59.
units.anchor: Instructors can use AI to create the first draft of a course syllabus

units.why: Says AI can generate 'quiz questions, study guides, or practice problems built from course content' for instructors, so P59 (instructor teaching work).
units.anchor: AI can also save instructors time by generating quiz questions, study guides, or practice problems

units.why: Says 'students can use AI tools independently to support their learning'; a general permission without conditions beyond support of learning, so P02.
units.anchor: students can use AI tools independently to support their learning
units.fit_note: Also states that instructor guidance is needed for course activities and assignments.

units.why: AI 'can serve as a tutor generating study aids such as flashcards, quizzes, and practice questions'; study-aid generation, so P14 rather than P12.
units.anchor: can serve as a tutor generating study aids such as flashcards, quizzes, and practice questions

units.why: AI tools 'can serve as a personal teaching assistant, explaining complex ideas that are difficult to understand'; tutor-like explanation of concepts, P12.
units.anchor: can serve as a personal teaching assistant, explaining complex ideas that are difficult to understand

units.why: AI can help with 'outlining, idea generation, and deeper engagement with concepts'; brainstorming and idea generation, P15.
units.anchor: AI can help students with outlining, idea generation, and deeper engagement with concepts

units.why: AI can serve 'as a writing tutor by shortening over-long text, improving spelling and grammar'; editing support, P91.
units.anchor: serve as a writing tutor by shortening over-long text, improving spelling and grammar

units.why: Wants students to use AI 'in ways that support their learning, without replacing the real work of learning how to learn'; the reason is protecting the practice that builds skill, P41.
units.anchor: without replacing the real work of learning how to learn

units.why: Says instructors should 'Define clear boundaries for AI use in course assignments and assessments'; an instruction to state expectations, P09.
units.anchor: Define clear boundaries for AI use in course assignments and assessments

units.why: Tells instructors to 'Remind students that AI-generated text and ideas must be cited appropriately'; a disclosure and citation expectation, P24.
units.anchor: AI-generated text and ideas must be cited appropriately
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors as a reminder to students; does not say how to cite.

units.why: Asks instructors to 'Help students understand why academic integrity standards exist'; explaining reasons to students, P66.
units.anchor: Help students understand why academic integrity standards exist

units.why: States 'AI outputs can be inaccurate, biased, or completely fabricated', a factual warning that outputs can be wrong, P31.
units.anchor: AI outputs can be inaccurate, biased, or completely fabricated

units.why: Tells instructors to 'help students to develop critical thinking skills and to practice evaluating AI-generated content'; verifying AI output, P31.
units.anchor: practice evaluating AI-generated content responsibly

units.why: Says faculty 'must be vigilant in preserving FERPA data and student privacy' with AI; personal-data protection, P50.
units.anchor: they must be vigilant in preserving FERPA data and student privacy

units.why: 'Faculty and students are encouraged to use campus-approved AI tools'; prefer vetted tools, coded P92 because it concerns institution-approved tools generally.
units.anchor: encouraged to use campus-approved AI tools

units.why: Says users should 'never share sensitive, or proprietary information with third-party tools'; data protection, P50.
units.anchor: never share sensitive, or proprietary information with third-party tools

units.why: Tells faculty to 'ensure that all students can access digital tools if assignments require them'; equal access, P51.
units.anchor: ensure that all students can access digital tools if assignments require them

units.why: Notes 'some digital tools may not be accessible' and to 'recommend campus-approved AI tools whenever possible'; accessibility of tools, P97.
units.anchor: Faculty should also be aware that some digital tools may not be accessible
units.fit_note: Also directs instructors to follow campus guidelines and recommend campus-approved tools.

units.why: Faculty 'have a responsibility to uphold the ethical, professional, and intellectual property standards'; a general conduct duty, P77.
units.anchor: uphold the ethical, professional, and intellectual property standards expected of university researchers and educators

units.why: Warns that 'AI tools are always collecting personal and proprietary information' and may breach laws; privacy risk, P50.
units.anchor: AI tools are always collecting personal and proprietary information during interactive or conversational use

units.why: Says campus tools 'can act as an idea partner to quickly draft learning outcomes, grading rubrics, slide decks'; instructor teaching work, P59.
units.anchor: can act as an idea partner to quickly draft learning outcomes, grading rubrics, slide decks

units.why: 'The knee-jerk response is to add a blanket AI policy to your syllabus, but this is not advised'; advises instructors against one blanket rule and for specific rules, so P04.
units.anchor: add a blanket AI policy to your syllabus, but this is not advised
units.fit_note: Advice against a blanket syllabus rule; does not itself say who decides.

units.why: Tells instructors to 'explain how and when it will be ok to use AI in class'; going beyond listing a rule, P66.
units.anchor: try to explain how and when it will be ok to use AI in class

units.why: Advises demonstrating 'key benefits and limitations of AI and show how AI writing differs from natural writing'; teaching about AI to students, P66.
units.anchor: key benefits and limitations of AI and show how AI writing differs from natural writing

units.why: 'Modify a few assignments so students can explore using AI tools in limited ways, such as for brainstorming or revision'; assignment redesign around AI, P35.
units.anchor: Modify a few assignments so students can explore using AI tools in limited ways

units.why: Says the goal of assignment makeovers 'is less about catching out students who are using AI' and more about 'creating new learning activities'; redesign instead of policing, P35.
units.anchor: less about catching out students who are using AI to do their assignments

units.why: 'Require students to make short informational presentations in class'; a concrete assignment redesign suggestion where students show understanding, P35.
units.anchor: Require students to make short informational presentations in class, alone, or in small groups

units.why: Suggests multimodal projects such as 'short podcasts, infographics, digital storybooks'; assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Ask students to create short podcasts, infographics, digital storybooks or graphic novels

units.why: 'CITL staff can help you design learning activities and assignments' offers consultation to instructors, P63.
units.anchor: CITL staff can help you design learning activities and assignments customized for your course content

units.why: CITL 'invites faculty and students to engage with us as we learn more about AI'; support offering, P63 (faculty-focused).
units.anchor: CITL invites faculty and students to engage with us as we learn more about AI
units.fit_note: Invitation extends to students, not only faculty.

documents.title: AI Guidance: Sample Statements for Engineering
tiers: Use When Instructed to Do So
documents.summary: The Grainger College of Engineering page offers four template syllabus statements (Restricted, Limited Use, Use When Instructed, All Use) and example statements from CS 411 and NIU. The college sets none of them as the rule; each instructor picks and fills in a template.
documents.stance_why: The page gives 'Template Statements for Engineering' in four tiers, from a full ban to 'welcome', and fills none in as the college rule. Because it offers tiers for instructors to choose, the stance is delegates with the tiers listed.

units.why: Introduces a set of named template statements (Restricted, Limited Use, Use When Instructed, All Use) for instructors to adopt; named tiers, P05.
units.anchor: Template Statements for Engineering

units.why: The Restricted template says tools 'are not permitted for any stage or phase of work in this class'; a default ban, P01.
units.anchor: are not permitted for any stage or phase of work in this class

units.why: 'Use of these tools in this course will be considered academic dishonesty and a violation of the University of Illinois Student Code'; classification as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: will be considered academic dishonesty and a violation of the University of Illinois Student Code

units.why: 'Any work written, developed, created, or inspired by artificial intelligence (AI) is considered plagiarism'; classes AI-derived work as plagiarism, P36.
units.anchor: Any work written, developed, created, or inspired by artificial intelligence (AI) is considered plagiarism

units.why: 'their use hinders the learning process and therefore is not allowed' gives learning as the reason for the ban, P41.
units.anchor: for this class their use hinders the learning process and therefore is not allowed

units.why: The Limited Use template: 'you must document and attribute all AI contributions to your coursework'; disclosure, P24.
units.anchor: you must document and attribute all AI contributions to your coursework

units.why: Students 'take full responsibility for the contributions including the accuracy of the information and reliability of sources'; ownership of submitted work, P29.
units.anchor: full responsibility for the contributions including the accuracy of the information and reliability of sources

units.why: 'keep a journal documenting prompts, AI responses, and your usage'; keeping a log of prompts and responses, P26.
units.anchor: keep a journal documenting prompts, AI responses, and your usage

units.why: The template leaves blanks for the instructor to 'Add acceptable uses here' and 'Add unacceptable uses here', so the instructor lists permitted and forbidden uses per course; P04, not P05 because no tier is defined by the list itself.
units.anchor: Add acceptable uses here, see suggestions in

units.why: 'If you have a question about the use of Generative AI, please reach out to your instructors'; ask when unsure, P10.
units.anchor: have a question about the use of Generative AI, please reach out to your instructors

units.why: 'Failure to abide by these guidelines is a violation of academic integrity'; misconduct classification, P36.
units.anchor: Failure to abide by these guidelines is a violation of academic integrity

units.why: 'We will investigate suspected uses of generative AI ... and apply sanctions as outlined in the University of Illinois Student Code'; a procedure routed through the Student Code, P81 rather than P37 because no concrete penalty is named.
units.anchor: investigate suspected uses of generative AI that do not follow these guidelines and apply sanctions

units.why: The Limited Use template opens with 'The appropriate use of generative AI varies from course to course'; use is set per course, P04.
units.anchor: The appropriate use of generative AI varies from course to course

units.why: The Use When Instructed template: 'You will be informed as to when, where, and how these tools are permitted'; the instructor decides per activity, P04.
units.anchor: be informed as to when, where, and how these tools are permitted to be used

units.why: 'Any use outside of when permission is explicitly given will be considered academic dishonesty'; the fallback when permission is absent, P06.
units.anchor: Any use outside of when permission is explicitly given will be considered academic dishonesty

units.why: The All Use template: tools 'are welcome in this class'; default permission, P02.
units.anchor: welcome in this class, provided that you cite when and how you use the tool
units.fit_note: Welcome is conditional on citing use.

units.why: The same sentence requires that you 'cite when and how you use the tool'; disclosure, P24 (the permission itself is the previous unit).
units.anchor: provided that you cite when and how you use the tool

units.why: 'You will be provided with examples of how to cite your use of this tool'; instructor supplies citation examples, P24.
units.anchor: provided with examples of how to cite your use of this tool for your assignments
units.fit_note: Promise by instructor to provide citation examples; it does not specify the citation contents.

units.why: 'AI programs are not a replacement for critical thinking, analysis, creativity, originality, and problem-solving'; students keep the thinking, P32.
units.anchor: AI programs are not a replacement for critical thinking, analysis, creativity, originality, and problem-solving

units.why: 'AI tools may be used to assist with engineering design as long as proper attribution is provided'; conditional permission for a use not listed in the types, so P02 with a note.
units.anchor: may be used to assist with engineering design as long as proper attribution is provided
units.fit_note: A permission for engineering design work conditional on attribution, rather than a global default.

units.why: The CS 411 example: 'Students are not allowed to use advanced automated tools' on assignments, a course ban, P01.
units.anchor: Students are not allowed to use advanced automated tools

units.why: It says AI 'is strictly prohibited for homework assignments and project track 2', setting rules per assessment, so P05 with a note.
units.anchor: strictly prohibited for homework assignments and project track 2
units.fit_note: Names which assignments are banned; the example does not define named tiers.

units.why: The CS 411 'allowed with attribution' option: use is allowed 'if that use is properly documented and credited'; disclosure, P24.
units.anchor: if that use is properly documented and credited

units.why: For group activities AI use 'is strongly discouraged and should be limited to debugging or seeking guidance'; discouragement without a ban, P03.
units.anchor: of generative AI is strongly discouraged and should be limited to debugging or seeking guidance

units.why: Use is 'conditional upon having made a genuine attempt to address the problem independently within your group'; try first, then AI, P90.
units.anchor: conditional upon having made a genuine attempt to address the problem independently within your group

units.why: 'any use of generative AI is clearly disclosed in your submission'; disclosure with each submission, P24.
units.anchor: any use of generative AI is clearly disclosed in your submission

units.why: 'Generative AI can be utilized to assist with front-end development tasks' in project track 1; code allowed under a stated condition, P16.
units.anchor: Generative AI can be utilized to assist with front-end development tasks

units.why: 'expressly forbidden for writing database-related code, including SQL queries, stored procedures, and triggers'; bans AI-produced code for named work, P19.
units.anchor: expressly forbidden for writing database-related code, including SQL queries, stored procedures, and triggers

units.why: The NIU example says predictive writing tools 'can be valuable writing tools in many contexts'; prose tools treated on their own terms, P18.
units.anchor: technologies (like ChatGPT, Google Translate, and Grammarly) can be valuable writing tools in many contexts

units.why: It says 'much of the learning in this course occurs through direct, personal experience of the writing process'; reason for care with AI, P41.
units.anchor: of the learning in this course occurs through direct, personal experience of the writing process

units.why: 'use them ethically by disclosing how you used them'; disclosure, P24.
units.anchor: use them ethically by disclosing how you used them

units.why: 'Regardless of what you use to compose, you are responsible for what you turn in'; P29.
units.anchor: you are responsible for what you turn in

units.why: Warns that 'inaccurate citations and sources from predictive technology puts you at risk of academic integrity violations'; students must check output, P31.
units.anchor: inaccurate citations and sources from predictive technology puts you at risk of academic integrity violations

documents.title: Using AI
documents.summary: This Grainger page sorts examples of appropriate and inappropriate AI use for teaching, learning and professional tasks around one test: augmenting versus replacing human thinking. It is advisory and mixes advice to instructors and students.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'If the intention of using AI is to augment human thinking, then it is likely an appropriate use' and gives many allowed uses (tutoring, proofreading, translation) with cautions. AI is allowed with conditions, so the stance is permit.

units.why: Sets the test for appropriate use: 'If the intention of using AI is to augment human thinking, then it is likely an appropriate use'. Students/staff keep the thinking, P32.
units.anchor: If the intention of using AI is to augment human thinking, then it is likely

units.why: 'If the intention of using AI is to replace human thinking, then it is likely an inappropriate use'; the limit side of the same test, P32.
units.anchor: If the intention of using AI is to replace human thinking, then it is likely

units.why: 'It is a good idea for students to use AI as a proofreader first'; editing and proofreading support, P91.
units.anchor: a good idea for students to use AI as a proofreader first

units.why: 'AI can be used for problem creation (e.g., homework), lesson planning, or grading rubrics'; instructor teaching work, P59.
units.anchor: AI can be used for problem creation (e.g., homework), lesson planning, or grading rubrics

units.why: 'Do not upload copyrighted or confidential course material to the AI'; a ban on uploading course material, P49.
units.anchor: Do not upload copyrighted or confidential course material to the AI

units.why: 'AI can create example data sets for various applications'; creating data for demonstrations, P59 (instructor teaching work).
units.anchor: AI can create example data sets for various applications

units.why: 'AI can assist in translating text between languages'; prose-related use, P18.
units.anchor: AI can assist in translating text between languages

units.why: 'AI can convert formats, such as from YAML to Markdown tables'; routine teaching-task use by instructors, P59.
units.anchor: AI can convert formats, such as from YAML to Markdown tables

units.why: 'Given an appropriate prompt, an LLM can function well as a tutor'; tutor use, P12.
units.anchor: Given an appropriate prompt, an LLM can function well as a tutor

units.why: Suggests copying in a homework and asking for 'a new one of the same difficulty level' for practice; practice problems, P14.
units.anchor: one of the same difficulty level and similar content so we can get more practice

units.why: 'it is helpful to give the LLM and example of the before and after'; practical prompting advice, P93.
units.anchor: it is helpful to give the LLM and example of the before and after

units.why: Names the first misuse category: 'the AI might give incorrect information that sounds right until inspected more closely'; P31.
units.anchor: the AI might give incorrect information that sounds right until inspected more closely

units.why: 'anything you upload to the AI could be used to train it' with 'implications for FERPA-protected information'; privacy risk, P50.
units.anchor: anything you upload to the AI could be used to train it

units.why: 'sometimes that is precisely what we are supposed to be doing' says avoiding thinking undermines the purpose of the task, P41.
units.anchor: strength of AI is it saves us from having to spend time thinking about things

units.why: 'Garbage in, garbage out' ties usefulness of output to prompt quality; prompting advice, P93.
units.anchor: usefulness and appropriateness of the LLM output depends heavily on the quality of the prompt

units.why: Says 'copy-pasting that summary as a concluding paragraph for a paper you have written could be problematic'; not submitting AI text as your own, P19.
units.anchor: that summary as a concluding paragraph for a paper you have written could be problematic

units.why: 'the human operator is ultimately responsible for checking the correctness of the output'; verification duty, P31.
units.anchor: the human operator is ultimately responsible for checking the correctness of the output

units.why: 'AI is not reliable for programming tasks that arent easily found on platforms like Stack Overflow'; limits of AI code, P31.
units.anchor: AI is not reliable for programming tasks

units.why: 'the human operator is ultimately responsible for the code and its operation'; ownership of code, P29.
units.anchor: the human operator is ultimately responsible for the code and its operation

units.why: 'You also need to be careful about FERPA protections' when using AI for letters; P50.
units.anchor: You also need to be careful about FERPA protections

units.why: 'AI should not be used to grade student assignments'; a ban on AI grading, P46.
units.anchor: AI should not be used to grade student assignments

units.why: Says teams 'trained a smaller LLM locally to grade specific assignments and have had good results'; an exception under local control, P101.
units.anchor: have trained a smaller LLM locally to grade specific assignments and have had good results
units.fit_note: Reported as an example, not as an approval rule.

units.why: 'AI is not suitable for writing peer reviews of academic manuscripts'; research and scholarship use, P62.
units.anchor: AI is not suitable for writing peer reviews of academic manuscripts

units.why: 'often not useful for learning because being shown the answer is not as useful as having to generate the answer yourself'; the reason against AI-solved homework, P41.
units.anchor: being shown the answer
units.fit_note: Applies the point to solving homework problems with AI.

units.why: 'Students generally prefer their professors to respond personally rather than using AI-generated replies'; advises against AI replies to students, P59.
units.anchor: Students generally prefer their professors to respond personally rather than using AI-generated replies

units.why: Warns recruiters 'will quickly develop the skill of recognizing the style that LLMs use'; a career reason not to submit unreworked AI text, P94.
units.anchor: they will quickly develop the skill of recognizing the style that LLMs use
units.fit_note: About job and application materials, not coursework.

notes: Coder B. Only the three screen=include documents were coded (CITL, Grainger guidance, Grainger Using AI); course documents were deferred. System-level Illinois guidance was inaccessible per the collect notes.
